opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, at the time I didn't really assess it in any rigorous way. I was an undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong, working on some early neural network projects, and I just had this intuition that the computation was mostly matrix operations, and GPUs were good at that. So I started writing CUDA code to train my own networks, thinking maybe this was a fairly novel thing to try.

It was only later, when I read more papers and talked with people, that I realized folks like Geoff Hinton's group and others were already doing this. Then AlexNet came out in 2012 and made it extremely clear that GPU-accelerated deep learning was not just recognized but was about to become *the* approach. So it was a bit of a humbling moment. I thought I'd stumbled onto something, and it turned out the field was already moving in that direction, and doing it at a much larger scale than I was.

But I don't regret it at all. Going through that process myself, actually writing the kernels, figuring out memory layouts, debugging why things were slow, gave me a very concrete understanding of how the hardware and the algorithms interact. That experience planted the seed for a lot of what I did later, in XGBoost, in MXNet, and especially in TVM, where the whole question is how to map machine learning workloads efficiently onto different hardware. So even though I wasn't first, learning by building it myself turned out to be really valuable.

r001.rationale: The candidate says that after reading more papers, Chen realized others were already using GPUs for deep learning, indicating the approach was likely recognized while he was developing his network.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, at the time I didn't do a very formal assessment. This was around 2010, when I was an undergrad at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, and I was trying to build a deep learning model for something like restricted Boltzmann machines and deep belief networks, since that was what was popular after Hinton's papers. The training was painfully slow on CPU, so my motivation was very practical: I just wanted my experiments to finish.

I did know there was some prior work. There were a couple of papers around 2009, from Andrew Ng's group at Stanford for example, showing that GPUs could speed up unsupervised deep learning by a large factor. So I knew the idea existed in principle, and that it wasn't crazy. But there was no framework you could just download and use. CUDA was fairly new, there was no cuDNN, and the tools basically consisted of CUBLAS and writing your own kernels. So the question of whether it was "recognized" was a bit abstract to me. The reality was that if I wanted to use it, I had to implement everything myself.

So the way I assessed it was by doing it. I wrote the matrix operations and the sampling steps in CUDA, got the model running on a gaming graphics card, and saw it was something like ten or more times faster than my CPU version. That was the real confirmation. And I think that experience shaped how I approached things later with CXXNet and then MXNet, because I realized the gap wasn't in the idea, it was in the engineering and the tooling. People knew GPUs could help; what was missing was infrastructure that made it easy for everyone to actually use them.

r001.rationale: The response cites 2009 papers demonstrating GPU acceleration for unsupervised deep learning and says this showed the idea was already known in principle.

astra-6.text: I wanted to understand whether this was just an idea I had or something people were already doing, so I looked for existing work on training neural networks with GPUs. Finding examples helped me realize that the general approach was already known. Then the question for my own network became more practical: how could I implement it efficiently, and what could I learn from those existing systems?

r001.rationale: The response says he looked for existing work and examples of training neural networks with GPUs, but it does not clearly identify research papers as the evidence.

sol-6.1.text: At the time, I wasn’t sure how widely people were already using GPUs for deep learning. So I looked through the literature and tried to understand what had been done. The key distinction was between something being possible and having tools that made it practical to build and train your own network. I wanted to understand both: whether people had demonstrated the speedup, and how accessible that approach was for someone trying to implement it.

r001.rationale: The response says Chen reviewed the literature to learn what had been done and whether GPU speedups had been demonstrated. It does not communicate that existing research papers were evidence that GPU acceleration was probably already recognized at the time.
